title: RAG Fundamentals: Retrieval Meets Generation
content: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pairs a language model with an external knowledge source so it can answer questions using information it was never trained on. Instead of relying only on what the model memorized during training, a RAG system retrieves relevant text chunks from a document store at query time and inserts them into the model's prompt as context. This course walks through the three core stages of a RAG pipeline: indexing (splitting source documents into chunks and storing them so they can be searched later), retrieval (given a user's question, finding the chunks most relevant to it), and generation (handing the retrieved chunks to the model along with the original question so it can produce a grounded answer). You'll learn why chunking strategy matters -- split documents at the wrong boundaries and you separate a question from its answer before the model even sees it -- and why 'stuffing everything into a huge context window' is not the same thing as RAG: a system with no retrieval step, just a large prompt, has no way to prioritize what's actually relevant, and costs far more in tokens. By the end of this course you'll be able to explain, in plain language, what problem RAG solves, what its three stages are, and one concrete failure mode that breaks the pipeline even when the underlying model is capable.

sections.heading: What problem this solves
sections.body: A language model's knowledge is frozen at training time and lives entirely inside its weights. That creates two problems the moment you want to use it on anything real: it doesn't know about your data (your company's return policy, last week's incident postmortem, a codebase that didn't exist when the model was trained), and even on topics it does know, it can state something confidently and wrongly with no way for you to check where the claim came from. Two tempting fixes don't actually work. Fine-tuning bakes new facts into the weights, but it's slow, expensive to redo every time the underlying data changes, and it still gives you no way to point at a source for any given answer. Just pasting your whole knowledge base into the prompt ("stuff it in the context window") seems simpler, but it doesn't scale past a small handful of documents, costs real money in tokens on every single call whether or not the content is relevant to the question asked, and -- as you'll see in "Where it breaks" below -- large models get measurably worse at using information buried in the middle of a long prompt. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is the practical middle path: keep the model's weights untouched, keep your knowledge base external and updatable, and at the moment of each question, retrieve only the small number of passages actually relevant to it and hand those to the model as context. The model still does the writing; it just isn't asked to write from memory alone.

sections.heading: How the pipeline actually works
sections.body: A RAG system has three distinct stages, and conflating them is the single most common source of confusion for people new to this. Indexing happens ahead of time, offline: your source documents (PDFs, wiki pages, support tickets, whatever) get split into chunks -- typically a few hundred tokens each -- and each chunk is run through an embedding model that turns it into a vector, a list of a few hundred to a few thousand floating-point numbers that captures the chunk's meaning geometrically. Chunks with similar meaning end up as nearby vectors in that space. Those vectors get stored in an index (a vector database, or even just an in-memory array for a small corpus) alongside the original chunk text. Retrieval happens live, per query: the user's question gets embedded with that same embedding model, and the index is searched for the chunks whose vectors are closest to the question's vector -- usually via cosine similarity -- returning the top handful ("top-k", commonly 3 to 10) candidate chunks. Generation is the final step: those retrieved chunks get assembled into a prompt alongside the original question -- something like "Using only the following passages, answer the question: [chunks] [question]" -- and handed to the language model, which writes the actual answer grounded in that supplied text rather than its own memorized weights. The mental model worth keeping: indexing is a librarian shelving books by subject, retrieval is pulling the three most relevant books off the shelf for a specific question, and generation is a researcher who's told to answer using only the books handed to them, not their own general knowledge.

sections.heading: Where it breaks
sections.body: Three failure modes account for most of the times a RAG system gives a wrong or unhelpful answer, and none of them are the model "being dumb" -- they're upstream problems in retrieval that generation can't recover from. Bad chunk boundaries are the most common: if a document gets split mechanically every N tokens with no regard for meaning, you can easily sever a fact from the sentence that qualifies it -- a chunk boundary that lands between "the refund window is 30 days" and "unless the item was purchased during the holiday sale, in which case it's 60" produces a chunk that's confidently wrong on its own. The fix is chunking that respects natural boundaries (paragraphs, sections) and often overlaps chunks slightly so a fact and its immediate context aren't split apart. Embedding similarity is not the same as relevance -- a chunk can be semantically close to a question's wording while being the wrong answer to what's actually being asked (a question about "return policy for electronics" can retrieve a chunk about "return policy for clothing" because the vector space clusters them as topically similar, even though the specific answer differs). This is why real systems often add a second, more precise re-ranking step after the initial vector-similarity retrieval rather than trusting embeddings alone. Finally, even with perfect retrieval, models exhibit a documented "lost in the middle" effect: they attend much more reliably to information at the very start or very end of a long prompt than to something buried in the middle of ten retrieved chunks -- which is a direct, measured argument for retrieving fewer, more relevant chunks rather than more, weaker ones.

sections.heading: A worked example
sections.body: Say your knowledge base is a company's internal policy documents, already chunked and indexed, and a support agent asks: "Can a customer return a laptop they bought 45 days ago?" At query time, that question is embedded into a vector. The retrieval step searches the index and returns its top three closest chunks by similarity: one stating "Standard returns are accepted within 30 days of purchase with proof of purchase," a second stating "Electronics purchased through the extended-warranty program may be returned within 90 days," and a third, less relevant chunk about the company's shipping carrier policy that happened to score just high enough to make the cut. The generation step receives all three chunks plus the original question, with an instruction to answer only from what's provided. A well-grounded answer says something like: "Under the standard policy, no -- the window is 30 days. However, if this laptop was purchased through the extended-warranty program, the return window extends to 90 days, so it's worth confirming which program applies before declining the return." Notice what happened: the model didn't have to guess or rely on memorized general knowledge about return policies -- it synthesized an answer strictly from the two relevant retrieved passages, correctly ignored the irrelevant shipping-carrier chunk instead of forcing it into the answer, and even surfaced the ambiguity (which program applies) rather than picking one silently. That's the actual value RAG delivers: not just an answer, but an answer traceable to specific source passages, with irrelevant retrieved noise correctly set aside.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.body: Everything above assumed chunking and retrieval just work correctly -- the next course in this track, on chunking strategies, is where you'll dig into exactly how to split documents so a chunk boundary doesn't sever a fact from its context, which is the single highest-leverage thing you can control in a RAG system's quality. After that, the evaluation course covers how teams actually measure whether a RAG system's retrieval and generation are working, rather than eyeballing a few outputs and hoping.

quiz.question: What are the three core stages of a RAG pipeline, in order?
options: Indexing, retrieval, generation
Training, fine-tuning, deployment
Generation, retrieval, indexing
Chunking, training, inference

quiz.question: Why is 'just stuffing everything into a huge context window' not the same as RAG?
options: It uses a different programming language
It has no retrieval step to prioritize what's relevant, and costs more tokens
It only works with images, not text
It requires a GPU cluster to run

quiz.question: Why does chunking strategy matter in a RAG system?
options: It doesn't matter, any chunk size works equally well
Bad chunk boundaries can separate a question from its answer before the model sees it
Chunking only affects how fast the UI renders
Chunking is only relevant for image data

title: RAG Bootcamp: From Fundamentals to Production Patterns
content: A bundled sequence covering RAG from first principles through common production pitfalls: what problem retrieval-augmented generation solves, how chunking and retrieval quality affect answer accuracy, and how teams evaluate whether a RAG system is actually working. Complete the linked courses in order.

title: RAG Practitioner Certification Assessment
content: This capstone assessment validates practical RAG knowledge across indexing, retrieval quality, and evaluation. Before attempting it, you should be comfortable explaining chunking tradeoffs, the difference between recall and precision in a retrieval step, and how to detect when a RAG system is hallucinating despite having the right document retrieved. The questions probe judgment calls, not just definitions: given a scenario where a RAG system retrieves the correct document but still gives a wrong answer, can you identify whether the fault lies in retrieval, prompt assembly, or the generation step itself? Passing this assessment is meant to signal you could debug a real RAG system in production, not just describe one in the abstract.

quiz.question: A RAG system retrieves the correct source document but still answers incorrectly. Where is the fault most likely to be?
options: Always the retriever
Could be prompt assembly or generation, not necessarily retrieval
Always the vector database
Always the chunk size

quiz.question: What does 'recall' measure in a retrieval step?
options: How fast the query runs
The fraction of relevant documents that were actually retrieved
How many tokens the answer uses
The model's temperature setting

quiz.question: Which of these is a sign a RAG system may be hallucinating despite good retrieval?
options: The answer cites the retrieved document accurately
The answer includes specific facts not present in any retrieved chunk
The answer is short
The answer takes longer to generate

quiz.question: What is this capstone primarily assessing?
options: Memorized definitions only
Practical judgment about where failures occur across the RAG pipeline
Typing speed
Knowledge of an unrelated programming language

title: Chunking Strategies: Splitting Documents Without Losing Meaning
content: How you split source documents into chunks determines whether retrieval can ever find the right answer, no matter how good your search algorithm is. This course compares fixed-size chunking (splitting every N characters or tokens, fast but blind to sentence and paragraph boundaries), recursive character splitting (trying paragraph breaks first, then sentences, then words, so chunks stay semantically coherent), and semantic chunking (using embedding similarity to find natural topic breaks). You'll learn the classic tradeoff: chunks that are too small lose surrounding context, so a retrieved sentence like 'it costs $49 per month' becomes useless without knowing what 'it' refers to; chunks that are too large dilute the embedding, mixing several topics into one vector so the chunk stops matching any single query well and wastes tokens on irrelevant text. You'll also learn why most production systems add overlap (for example a 50-100 token overlap between consecutive chunks) so that a fact sitting right at a boundary still appears intact in at least one chunk.

quiz.question: What is the main problem with chunks that are too small?
options: They take longer to embed
They can lose the surrounding context needed to make sense of the retrieved fact
They are always more expensive to store
They can't be indexed at all

quiz.question: Why do production RAG systems often use overlapping chunks?
options: To make the vector database file larger for no reason
So a fact sitting near a chunk boundary still appears intact in at least one chunk
Overlap speeds up the language model's inference
Overlap is required by every embedding model's API

quiz.question: A document is split into 300-token chunks with zero overlap, and a key fact spans the last 20 tokens of one chunk and the first 30 of the next. What is the likely outcome?
options: Retrieval will always find both chunks together
Neither chunk alone may contain the complete fact, hurting retrieval quality
The embedding model will automatically merge them
This has no effect on RAG performance

title: Evaluating RAG Systems: Beyond 'Does the Answer Look Right?'
content: A RAG system can fail in the retriever, the generator, or both, and eyeballing final answers rarely tells you which. This course introduces the standard split between retrieval metrics and generation metrics. Retrieval metrics like precision (what fraction of retrieved chunks are actually relevant) and recall (what fraction of relevant chunks were retrieved) tell you whether the search step is working, independent of what the model does with the results. Generation metrics like faithfulness (does the answer only state things supported by the retrieved chunks) and answer relevance (does the answer actually address the question) tell you whether the model used good context well. You'll learn why a golden dataset of representative questions with known correct answers and known relevant source chunks is essential: without it you can't separate 'the retriever found the wrong document' from 'the retriever found the right document but the model ignored it.' You'll also see why automated frameworks (like RAGAS-style faithfulness scoring using an LLM judge) are useful for catching regressions at scale, but should be spot-checked against human judgment.

quiz.question: A RAG system gives a wrong answer. Retrieval metrics show high recall for that query. What does this suggest?
options: The retriever is definitely broken
The problem is more likely in generation (the model ignored or misused good context)
The vector database is corrupted
Nothing can be concluded

quiz.question: What does a 'faithfulness' metric measure in RAG evaluation?
options: How fast the answer was generated
Whether the answer only states things supported by the retrieved chunks
How many chunks were retrieved
The size of the embedding model

quiz.question: Why is a golden dataset with known relevant chunks important for RAG evaluation?
options: It lets you separate retrieval failures from generation failures
It's only needed for marketing purposes
It replaces the need for any retrieval step
It guarantees zero hallucinations

title: Vector Databases: How Similarity Search Actually Works
content: Vector databases store embeddings (numeric representations of text meaning) and let you ask 'which stored vectors are closest to this query vector?' at scale. This course covers why exact nearest-neighbor search becomes too slow once you have millions of vectors, and how approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms like HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs) trade a small amount of accuracy for massive speed gains by building a graph structure that lets search skip most of the dataset. You'll learn why cosine similarity (or dot product on normalized vectors) is the standard distance metric for text embeddings, how embedding dimensionality (384, 768, 1536, etc.) affects both storage cost and retrieval quality, and why metadata filtering (restricting search to, say, documents from the last 30 days or a specific customer) needs to be combined carefully with vector search rather than applied as an afterthought. You'll also learn when a vector database is overkill: if your corpus is small or queries are mostly exact keyword lookups, a simpler full-text search index can outperform embeddings on both cost and accuracy.

quiz.question: Why do production systems use approximate nearest neighbor search instead of exact search?
options: Approximate search is always more accurate
Exact search becomes too slow at scale; ANN trades a little accuracy for large speed gains
Exact search doesn't work with embeddings at all
ANN is required by law for AI systems

quiz.question: When might a vector database be the wrong choice for a search problem?
options: Never, vector search is always superior
When the corpus is small or queries are mostly exact keyword lookups, where full-text search may do better
When you have more than 100 documents
When you need any kind of filtering

quiz.question: What is a key risk of bolting metadata filtering onto vector search as an afterthought?
options: It has no effect on results
It can silently return irrelevant results or miss relevant ones if the filter and similarity search aren't combined correctly
It always doubles storage costs
It disables cosine similarity entirely

title: Agentic RAG: Retrieval as a Tool, Not a Fixed Pipeline Step
content: Classic RAG retrieves once, then generates once -- a fixed pipeline. Agentic RAG instead gives the model retrieval as a tool it can call repeatedly and reason about, which matters for multi-hop questions that no single retrieval pass can answer (for example, 'which of our vendors had the highest renewal cost increase compared to last year's contract?' requires finding two separate documents and comparing them). This course covers iterative retrieve-reason loops where the model decides whether it has enough evidence yet or needs to search again with a refined query, query decomposition (breaking a complex question into sub-questions that are each independently retrievable), and query rewriting (reformulating a vague user question into a more retrievable form before searching). You'll also learn about self-critique patterns, where the model checks its own draft answer against the retrieved evidence before finalizing, catching cases where it drifted from the sources. The core judgment call this course builds: recognizing when a question is genuinely multi-hop (static single-shot RAG will fail) versus when it just looks complex but is answerable from one good retrieval.

quiz.question: What distinguishes agentic RAG from classic single-shot RAG?
options: Agentic RAG never uses embeddings
The model can call retrieval repeatedly and decide whether it has enough evidence, rather than retrieving once and generating once
Agentic RAG is only for image data
There is no difference, just marketing

quiz.question: Why does a multi-hop question like comparing two vendor contracts challenge classic single-shot RAG?
options: It requires finding and combining evidence from separate retrieval steps that one search pass won't surface together
Multi-hop questions are always shorter than single-hop ones
Classic RAG can't handle numbers
It requires a different embedding model entirely

quiz.question: What is 'query decomposition' in an agentic RAG system?
options: Deleting the user's original query
Breaking a complex question into sub-questions that are each independently retrievable
Compressing the vector database
A method for fine-tuning the generator model

title: Hybrid Search and Reranking: When Embeddings Alone Aren't Enough
content: Dense embedding search is excellent at matching meaning but surprisingly weak at exact-match lookups: a query for a specific model number, error code, or product SKU can retrieve semantically 'close' but factually wrong chunks because embeddings compress away rare tokens. Hybrid search combines dense vector search with sparse keyword search (commonly BM25, a classic term-frequency ranking algorithm) and merges the two ranked lists, so exact terms still surface even when their embedding neighbors look similar. This course also covers reranking: after an initial retrieval step returns, say, the top 50 candidate chunks cheaply, a more expensive cross-encoder model rescoring the query against each candidate individually can reorder them far more accurately than the original similarity score, because a cross-encoder actually reads the query and chunk together rather than comparing pre-computed vectors. You'll learn the practical pattern: cheap broad retrieval first, expensive precise reranking second, applied only to a small candidate set to keep latency and cost reasonable.

quiz.question: Why might a query for an exact product SKU fail with pure dense embedding search?
options: Embeddings compress away rare or exact tokens, so semantically 'close' but factually wrong chunks can outrank the exact match
Dense search cannot process numbers at all
SKUs are too long to embed
This never happens in practice

quiz.question: What is the typical two-stage pattern for combining retrieval and reranking?
options: Rerank first on the whole corpus, then retrieve
Cheap broad retrieval over the full corpus first, then expensive precise reranking on a small candidate set
Only ever use one stage
Reranking replaces retrieval entirely

quiz.question: Why is a cross-encoder reranker generally more accurate than the original similarity score, but also more expensive?
options: It reads the query and each candidate chunk together instead of comparing pre-computed vectors, which costs more compute per comparison
It uses a smaller model with fewer parameters
It skips the embedding step entirely for free
Cross-encoders are not actually more accurate

title: What Is an LLM, Really?
content: A large language model is, at its core, a statistical model trained to predict the next token given the tokens before it, learned from an enormous corpus of text. This course demystifies what that means in practice: the model has no database of facts it looks up, no memory of specific training documents it can cite, and no built-in notion of 'true' versus 'false' -- it has learned patterns of what text tends to follow other text, at a scale detailed enough that those patterns encode a remarkable amount of world knowledge and reasoning-like behavior. You'll learn why this framing explains both LLM strengths (fluent, context-sensitive generation across almost any topic) and their characteristic weaknesses (confident-sounding fabrication when the learned patterns don't actually contain the answer, sensitivity to how a question is phrased, and no reliable way to know what it doesn't know). Understanding an LLM as 'next-token prediction at scale' rather than as a search engine or a reasoning engine is the single most useful mental model for predicting when it will succeed and when it will quietly fail.

quiz.question: What is the most accurate description of what an LLM fundamentally does?
options: Looks up facts in an internal database
Predicts the next token given prior tokens, based on patterns learned from training text
Executes retrieval queries against the internet in real time
Runs a symbolic logic engine over the input

quiz.question: Why can an LLM produce confident-sounding but false statements?
options: It deliberately tries to deceive users
It generates plausible-sounding text based on learned patterns, with no built-in fact-checking against a source of truth
It is copying errors from a corrupted database
This only happens with very old models

quiz.question: Why is 'next-token prediction at scale' a more useful mental model than 'search engine' for predicting LLM behavior?
options: Because it explains both fluent generation and confident fabrication as two sides of the same mechanism
Because search engines are technically identical to LLMs
Because it means the model always tells the truth
It isn't useful; both models are equivalent

title: Tokens, Context Windows, and Why They Matter
content: Language models don't read text character by character or word by word -- they read tokens, chunks of text produced by a tokenizer (commonly byte-pair encoding), where a token might be a whole common word, a word fragment, or even a single punctuation mark. This course explains why 'the quick brown fox' might be 4 tokens while an uncommon word like 'antidisestablishmentarianism' could be split into 6 or more, and why this matters for both cost (providers bill per token) and behavior (models can be worse at character-level tasks like counting letters, because they never see individual characters). You'll also learn what a context window is: the maximum number of tokens (input plus output combined, for most APIs) a model can process in one call, and what happens when you exceed it -- either an error, or silent truncation of the oldest content, depending on the system. You'll leave able to estimate roughly how many tokens a piece of text will consume and explain why a bigger context window isn't free: it increases both cost and, past a point, the risk that the model pays less attention to content buried in the middle.

quiz.question: Why can an LLM sometimes struggle with a task like counting the letters in a word?
options: It never learned the alphabet
It processes text as tokens, which often don't correspond to individual characters
It's a hardware limitation
This never actually happens

quiz.question: What typically happens when your input plus expected output would exceed a model's context window?
options: The model automatically upgrades itself
You get an error or the oldest content gets silently truncated, depending on the system
Nothing, all systems handle this perfectly by default
The model pauses and waits for more memory

quiz.question: Why isn't a bigger context window simply 'free' upside with no downside?
options: Larger context windows are illegal in some countries
It increases cost and can increase the risk the model pays less attention to content buried in the middle
Bigger context windows make the model slower to install
There is no downside, bigger is strictly better

title: Choosing the Right Model for the Job
content: There is no single 'best' model -- only the best model for a given task, latency budget, and cost target. This course walks through a practical decision framework: start with task complexity (a simple classification or extraction task rarely needs a frontier reasoning model), then consider latency requirements (a real-time chat interface has very different tolerance than a nightly batch job), then cost at your expected volume (a 10x cost difference matters enormously at scale and barely at all for a prototype), then special requirements like reliable structured output, tool-calling ability, or a very long context window. You'll learn why teams frequently over-provision -- reaching for the largest, most expensive model by default -- and why a smaller model with a well-engineered prompt and good few-shot examples often matches a frontier model's accuracy on a narrow, well-specified task at a fraction of the cost and latency. You'll also learn to recognize the opposite mistake: under-provisioning on tasks that genuinely require strong multi-step reasoning, where a cheaper model fails silently by producing plausible-looking but wrong output.

quiz.question: Why might a smaller, cheaper model be the right choice for a narrow, well-specified task?
options: Smaller models are always more accurate
With good prompting and examples, a smaller model can match a frontier model's accuracy on narrow tasks at much lower cost and latency
Larger models cannot be used for simple tasks at all
This is never true in practice

quiz.question: What is a common mistake teams make when selecting a model?
options: Always choosing the cheapest option regardless of task
Over-provisioning by defaulting to the largest, most expensive model even for simple tasks
Never considering latency at all
Testing multiple models before committing

quiz.question: What is a risk of under-provisioning on a task that requires genuine multi-step reasoning?
options: The system will always crash with a visible error
The cheaper model may fail silently, producing plausible-looking but incorrect output
Nothing, cost is the only relevant factor
The task will simply run faster

title: Reading a Model Card
content: A model card is a provider's documentation summarizing a model's training data, intended uses, known limitations, benchmark performance, and safety evaluations -- and learning to read one critically is a core skill for picking models responsibly. This course covers what to look for: training data composition and cutoff date (does it know about recent events or your domain's jargon), stated intended use and out-of-scope uses (a model card explicitly warning against medical or legal advice use is a real signal, not boilerplate), and benchmark scores presented with context (a leaderboard number without knowing which exact benchmark version, whether the test set could have leaked into training data, or whether the benchmark measures anything relevant to your use case, is close to meaningless on its own). You'll also learn to look for license terms, since some 'open' models restrict commercial use or require attribution, and safety evaluation summaries, which tell you what red-teaming was done and what failure modes are already known before you ever run the model yourself.

quiz.question: Why should a benchmark score on a model card be read with skepticism rather than taken at face value?
options: Benchmark scores are always fabricated
Without knowing the exact benchmark, possible test-set contamination, and relevance to your use case, the number alone tells you little
Benchmarks never change over time
Model cards don't include benchmarks

quiz.question: Why does a model card's 'out-of-scope uses' section matter?
options: It's just legal boilerplate with no practical meaning
It signals real limitations, like explicitly warning against medical or legal advice use
It only applies to open-weight models
It replaces the need for any testing

quiz.question: What should you check on a model card before assuming you can use a model commercially?
options: The color scheme of the documentation
The license terms, since some 'open' models restrict commercial use
The number of parameters only
Nothing, all models can be used commercially

title: Open-Weight vs. Closed Models
content: Open-weight models (like Llama or Mistral) publish their trained parameters for anyone to download, run, and fine-tune, while closed models (like GPT, Claude, or Gemini) are only accessible through a provider's API. This course covers the real tradeoffs behind that choice: open-weight models give you full control over hosting, data privacy (nothing leaves your infrastructure), and the ability to fine-tune on proprietary data, at the cost of you owning all the infrastructure, scaling, and reliability engineering yourself. Closed models typically offer the most capable frontier performance and zero infrastructure burden, but you're sending data to a third party, subject to their rate limits, pricing changes, and deprecation schedules. You'll learn a key nuance often missed: 'open' doesn't always mean 'free to use however you want' -- some open-weight licenses restrict commercial use above a certain scale or require attribution, so the licensing terms matter as much as the technical access model. You'll leave able to match a project's constraints (data sensitivity, budget, need for customization, team's infra capacity) to the right category.

quiz.question: What is a key benefit of open-weight models over closed API-only models?
options: They are always more accurate
They give you control over hosting and data privacy since nothing needs to leave your infrastructure
They never have any licensing restrictions
They require no engineering effort at all

quiz.question: What is a common misconception about 'open' models?
options: That they are all trained the same way
That 'open' always means unrestricted commercial use, when some licenses restrict scale or require attribution
That they can never be fine-tuned
That they are always smaller than closed models

quiz.question: A team has strict data-residency requirements and in-house ML infrastructure. Which model category is likely a better fit?
options: A closed API-only model, regardless of requirements
An open-weight model they can self-host to keep data in-house
Neither option can satisfy data-residency requirements
The choice has no bearing on data residency

title: How LLMs Generate Text: Autoregression and Sampling
content: LLMs generate text one token at a time, feeding each generated token back in as input to predict the next one -- a process called autoregressive generation. At each step, the model produces a probability distribution over its entire vocabulary (via a softmax function), and a sampling strategy decides which token to actually pick. This course covers the key sampling parameters that shape output: temperature (scaling the distribution -- low temperature makes the model pick high-probability tokens almost deterministically, high temperature flattens the distribution toward more surprising, creative choices), top-p / nucleus sampling (only sampling from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p, cutting off the unlikely long tail), and top-k (restricting sampling to only the k most likely tokens). You'll learn why 'hallucination' is not a separate bug bolted onto an otherwise-truthful system, but a natural consequence of a model that is always generating the statistically plausible next token -- there is no built-in step where it checks generated content against ground truth, so a fluent, grammatically perfect sentence can still be entirely fabricated.

quiz.question: What does 'autoregressive' mean in the context of LLM text generation?
options: The model generates the entire response at once
The model generates one token at a time, feeding each output back in to predict the next
The model only works on regression problems, not text
The model regenerates its own weights during inference

quiz.question: What effect does a higher temperature setting have on generation?
options: It makes the model deterministic and always pick the single most likely token
It flattens the probability distribution, increasing the chance of more surprising or creative token choices
It has no effect on output at all
It only affects how fast tokens are generated

quiz.question: Why is hallucination best understood as a natural consequence of how LLMs generate text, rather than a separate bug?
options: Because the model is deliberately programmed to lie
Because the model always generates the statistically plausible next token with no built-in fact-check against ground truth
Because hallucination only occurs due to hardware errors
Because it only happens with very small models

title: Prompting Basics: Structure, Examples, and Output Format
content: A well-structured prompt reliably improves output quality more than almost any other lever available to you, and this course covers the foundational structure: clear task instructions stated up front, relevant context the model needs to complete the task, and an explicit description of the desired output format (a JSON schema, a specific list length, a tone). You'll learn about few-shot prompting -- including one or more worked examples of input-and-desired-output pairs directly in the prompt -- and why it often outperforms lengthy abstract instructions, because showing the model exactly what 'good' looks like removes ambiguity that a written description can leave open. You'll also learn the difference between a system prompt (persistent instructions that apply across a whole conversation, like persona or constraints) and a user prompt (the specific task or question at hand) at a high level -- this course introduces the distinction, while the Context Engineering track goes deeper on how to actually architect what goes into each. A recurring theme: specificity beats generality; a vague instruction like 'be helpful' produces far less consistent output than a precise one describing exactly what a good answer contains.

quiz.question: Why does few-shot prompting (showing worked examples) often outperform long abstract instructions?
options: Examples are always shorter than instructions
Showing exactly what 'good' output looks like removes ambiguity that written descriptions can leave open
Few-shot prompting uses a different model entirely
It doesn't outperform abstract instructions in practice

quiz.question: What is the practical difference between a system prompt and a user prompt at a high level?
options: There is no difference
A system prompt holds persistent instructions/persona across a conversation, while a user prompt is the specific task at hand
A system prompt is always shorter than a user prompt
User prompts are only used for images

quiz.question: Why does a vague instruction like 'be helpful' tend to produce less consistent output than a specific one?
options: Vague instructions are technically invalid JSON
It leaves the model to guess what 'helpful' means in this context, versus a precise description of what a good answer contains
The model ignores vague instructions entirely
Vague instructions cost more tokens

title: Fine-Tuning vs. Prompting vs. RAG: Choosing the Right Lever
content: Teams often reach for fine-tuning to solve problems that prompting or RAG would solve faster and cheaper, and this course builds the judgment to tell them apart. Prompt engineering (including few-shot examples) is fast to iterate, requires no training infrastructure, and is the right first step for most problems, especially ones about format, tone, or task framing. RAG is the right tool when the problem is 'the model doesn't know this specific fact or this changed recently' -- it injects fresh, retrievable knowledge without touching the model's weights. Fine-tuning changes the model's weights on a custom dataset, and it's the right tool for a narrower set of problems: teaching a very consistent output style or format the model doesn't reliably produce even with good prompting, adapting to a specialized vocabulary or writing style at scale, or reducing prompt length (and therefore cost) for a repeated task once you know the exact desired behavior. You'll learn the common mistake: fine-tuning on facts, hoping the model will 'know' new information reliably -- fine-tuning is poor at reliably injecting new factual knowledge and terrible at keeping that knowledge current, which is exactly what RAG is built for instead.

quiz.question: What is fine-tuning generally the wrong tool for?
options: Teaching a consistent output format
Reliably injecting new, frequently-changing factual knowledge into the model
Adapting to a specialized vocabulary
Reducing prompt length for a repeated task

quiz.question: When is RAG the better choice over fine-tuning?
options: When you need the model to know specific facts that change frequently over time
When you want to change the model's output tone permanently
When you have no data to work with at all
RAG and fine-tuning solve identical problems

quiz.question: Why is prompt engineering usually the right first step before considering fine-tuning?
options: It requires training infrastructure
It's fast to iterate and solves a large share of problems, especially around format and framing, without touching model weights
It's slower than fine-tuning
Prompting never works for format-related problems

title: Embeddings Explained: Turning Meaning Into Vectors
content: An embedding model converts a piece of text into a fixed-length vector of numbers positioned so that semantically similar text ends up close together in that vector space -- 'a friendly dog' and 'a happy puppy' land nearer each other than either does to 'quarterly tax filing.' This course covers how embedding models are typically trained using contrastive learning (pulling similar pairs closer, pushing dissimilar pairs apart) and how the resulting vectors get used: similarity search (the backbone of RAG retrieval), clustering (grouping similar documents without labels), and classification (using vector distance to a set of labeled examples). You'll learn the important distinction between an embedding model and a generative LLM: an embedding model doesn't generate text at all, it only produces a numeric representation, and the two are often entirely different model architectures even when offered by the same provider. You'll also learn about the practical tradeoff in embedding dimensionality -- higher-dimensional vectors (1536 or more) can capture finer-grained distinctions but cost more to store and search, while smaller vectors (384-768) are cheaper and often sufficient for narrower domains.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental difference between an embedding model and a generative LLM?
options: There is no difference, they're interchangeable
An embedding model produces a numeric vector representing meaning; it does not generate text
Embedding models are always larger than generative models
Generative models cannot use embeddings at all

quiz.question: What is the practical tradeoff of using a higher-dimensional embedding (e.g. 1536) versus a smaller one (e.g. 384)?
options: Higher dimensions are always strictly worse
Higher dimensions can capture finer distinctions but cost more to store and search
Dimensionality has no effect on cost or quality
Smaller embeddings can't be used for search at all

quiz.question: How are embedding models typically trained to place similar text close together in vector space?
options: Contrastive learning, pulling similar pairs closer and pushing dissimilar pairs apart
Random initialization with no training at all
By memorizing a lookup table of every possible sentence
By fine-tuning on labeled sentiment data only

title: Scaling Laws and Their Limits
content: Scaling laws describe an empirical relationship: as you increase model parameters, training data, and compute together in the right proportions, a model's training loss decreases in a predictable, smooth curve. This course covers the Chinchilla-style finding that many earlier large models were undertrained relative to their size -- for a fixed compute budget, a smaller model trained on proportionally more data often outperforms a larger model trained on less data. You'll learn why scaling laws predict smooth improvement in loss, but do not straightforwardly predict which specific capabilities will appear or when -- the debate over 'emergent abilities' (capabilities that seem to appear suddenly past a certain scale rather than improving gradually) is contested precisely because it's unclear how much of that appearance is a real phenomenon versus an artifact of how a capability is measured. You'll leave with the practical implication: bigger is not automatically better for a given deployment, because scaling laws describe training loss on average, not whether a larger model is worth its extra latency and cost for your specific, narrower task, where a smaller well-trained model may already saturate the metrics you actually care about.

quiz.question: What did Chinchilla-style scaling law research find about many earlier large models?
options: They were perfectly optimally trained
Many were undertrained relative to their size; a smaller model on proportionally more data could outperform them for the same compute budget
Model size has no relationship to training data needs
Larger models always need less data

quiz.question: Why is the debate over 'emergent abilities' contested among researchers?
options: Because scaling laws are entirely disproven
Because it's unclear how much apparent sudden capability jumps are real versus artifacts of how the capability is measured
Because no one has ever measured model capabilities before
Because emergent abilities only apply to embedding models

quiz.question: Why doesn't a scaling law finding that bigger models have lower average training loss mean 'always deploy the biggest model'?
options: Scaling laws are only theoretical and never validated
A smaller, well-trained model may already saturate the metrics that matter for a specific narrow task, at lower latency and cost
Bigger models are always cheaper to run
Training loss and deployment value are the same thing

title: Inference Optimization: KV Caching, Batching, and Quantization
content: Running a trained model efficiently at inference time is a distinct engineering problem from training it, and this course covers the core techniques that make production LLM serving affordable. KV (key-value) caching stores the attention keys and values computed for earlier tokens so each new token generation step doesn't have to recompute attention over the entire prior sequence from scratch -- without it, autoregressive generation would get quadratically slower as output grows. Batching groups multiple concurrent requests together so the GPU processes them in parallel rather than one at a time, dramatically improving throughput at the cost of some added latency per individual request. Quantization reduces the numerical precision of model weights (from 16-bit down to 8-bit or 4-bit representations), shrinking memory footprint and speeding up computation at a small, often acceptable cost in output quality. You'll also learn why inference cost is frequently bottlenecked by memory bandwidth (how fast weights can be read from memory) rather than raw compute, which is why techniques like speculative decoding (using a small draft model to propose several tokens that a larger model verifies in one pass) can meaningfully speed up generation.

quiz.question: What problem does KV caching solve during autoregressive generation?
options: It reduces the number of parameters in the model
It avoids recomputing attention over the entire prior sequence for every new token, preventing quadratic slowdown
It compresses the model's weights permanently
It eliminates the need for a GPU

quiz.question: Why is inference often bottlenecked by memory bandwidth rather than raw compute?
options: GPUs have no memory bandwidth limits
Reading model weights from memory fast enough is often the limiting factor, which is why techniques like speculative decoding help
Compute is always the bottleneck, never memory
This is only true for CPUs, not GPUs

quiz.question: What tradeoff does quantization introduce?
options: It has no tradeoffs, only benefits
It reduces memory footprint and speeds up computation, at a small often-acceptable cost in output quality
It always doubles the model's accuracy
It only works for training, not inference

title: LLM Fundamentals Certification Assessment
content: This capstone validates core LLM fundamentals judgment across model mechanics, deployment tradeoffs, and model selection. Before attempting it you should be comfortable explaining autoregressive generation and why it produces confident fabrication, the practical differences between fine-tuning, prompting, and RAG as levers for changing model behavior, how scaling laws relate to real deployment decisions, and the tradeoffs between open-weight and closed models. The questions are scenario-based: given a team defaulting to the largest available model for a simple classification task, can you identify the likely inefficiency and a better alternative? Given a team fine-tuning to inject fast-changing facts, can you identify why that approach will keep going stale? Passing signals you can make sound, cost-aware model and technique choices in a real project, not just recite definitions.

quiz.question: A team fine-tunes a model weekly to keep it updated on fast-changing product prices. What is the core problem with this approach?
options: Fine-tuning is illegal for factual data
Fine-tuning is a poor mechanism for keeping frequently-changing facts current; RAG is better suited to this
Fine-tuning is always faster than RAG
There is no problem with this approach

quiz.question: A simple sentiment classification task is routed to the largest, most expensive frontier model by default. What's the likely issue?
options: This is optimal and should always be done
It's likely over-provisioned; a smaller model with good prompting could match accuracy at far lower cost and latency
Large models cannot perform classification tasks
Sentiment classification requires the largest model available

quiz.question: Why does an LLM's autoregressive, next-token nature make hallucination an inherent risk rather than a rare bug?
options: Because it generates the statistically plausible next token with no built-in ground-truth check
Because hallucination is caused by a separate faulty subsystem
Because only fine-tuned models hallucinate
Because hallucination only occurs at high temperature settings

quiz.question: What is this capstone primarily assessing?
options: Ability to recite textbook definitions verbatim
Practical, scenario-based judgment about model behavior, technique selection, and deployment tradeoffs
Speed of prompt writing
Knowledge of an unrelated domain

title: What Is a Multi-Agent System?
content: A multi-agent system uses two or more distinct LLM-powered agents, each with its own role, instructions, and often its own tools, that coordinate to complete a task no single agent handles as well alone. This course introduces the core idea by contrasting it with a single agent with many tools: a single research-and-writing agent juggling fact lookup, outlining, and prose polishing in one prompt tends to do all three adequately but none excellently, while splitting the work into a researcher agent, an outliner agent, and a writer agent -- each with a narrow, well-defined job and a prompt tuned specifically for it -- often produces better results per step, at the cost of added coordination complexity and latency. You'll learn the common introductory patterns: pipeline (agents run in a fixed sequence, each consuming the previous one's output), manager-worker (one orchestrator agent decides what to delegate and to whom), and debate (multiple agents propose and critique each other's answers before converging). The judgment call this course builds: recognizing when a problem is complex and heterogeneous enough to benefit from splitting across agents, versus when it's simple enough that a single well-prompted agent is faster, cheaper, and just as good.

quiz.question: What is a core motivation for splitting a task across multiple specialized agents instead of one general agent?
options: It's always cheaper to run more agents
A narrowly-scoped agent with a tuned prompt for one job often outperforms one agent juggling many different jobs at once
Multi-agent systems eliminate the need for any prompting
It reduces the total number of API calls needed

quiz.question: What is the 'manager-worker' multi-agent pattern?
options: Agents run in a strict fixed sequence with no decision-making
One orchestrator agent decides what to delegate and to which specialist agent
All agents run completely independently with no coordination
A pattern used only for image generation

quiz.question: When might a single well-prompted agent be a better choice than a multi-agent system?
options: Never, multi-agent is always superior
When the task is simple enough that added coordination complexity and latency from multiple agents isn't worth it
Only when the budget is unlimited
Single agents cannot use tools

title: Orchestrator vs. Swarm: Two Coordination Patterns
content: Multi-agent systems generally coordinate in one of two broad shapes: centralized orchestration, where a single planning agent decides the task breakdown and explicitly delegates each piece to the right specialist agent, or decentralized swarm coordination, where peer agents communicate and negotiate among themselves without a designated controller. This course covers the tradeoffs: orchestrator patterns are more predictable and easier to debug (there's one place to look for 'why did the system decide this'), but the orchestrator becomes a single point of failure and a potential bottleneck as task complexity grows. Swarm patterns can be more resilient (no single agent's failure stops everything) and can scale to more agents more gracefully, but are harder to reason about and debug, since the emergent behavior comes from many local interactions rather than one visible plan. You'll learn that most production systems today lean orchestrator-style because predictability and debuggability matter enormously when real money or user-facing decisions are on the line, and true decentralized swarms remain more common in research settings than in shipped products.

quiz.question: What is a key advantage of the orchestrator pattern over a swarm pattern?
options: It scales infinitely with zero bottlenecks
It's more predictable and easier to debug since there's one place to inspect the decision-making
It never fails
It requires no planning agent at all

quiz.question: What is a key risk of the centralized orchestrator pattern?
options: It has no risks at all
The orchestrator can become a single point of failure and a bottleneck as complexity grows
It cannot delegate tasks to specialist agents
It always produces worse results than swarms

quiz.question: Why do most production multi-agent systems today lean toward orchestrator-style coordination rather than true decentralized swarms?
options: Swarms are technically impossible to build
Predictability and debuggability matter a great deal when real decisions or money are on the line
Orchestrators are always cheaper to run
Swarms require more agents than orchestrators

title: Agent Communication: How Agents Actually Pass State
content: As soon as you have more than one agent, you need a concrete answer to 'how does agent B find out what agent A learned?' This course covers the main mechanisms: shared memory or a blackboard (a common store all agents read from and write to, useful when many agents need visibility into evolving shared state), direct message passing (agent A's output is explicitly routed as agent B's input, giving tight control over exactly what each agent sees), and structured handoff objects (rather than passing raw conversation transcripts, agents pass a defined schema -- like 'findings: [...], open_questions: [...], confidence: 0.8' -- that the next agent can reliably parse). You'll learn why naively concatenating the entire conversation history and handing it to every subsequent agent breaks down as systems grow: it burns context window and cost on irrelevant history, and buries the specific handoff information the next agent actually needs inside a wall of text it has to re-derive relevance from. You'll also learn why this is a genuinely emerging area -- protocols standardizing how agents discover and call each other's capabilities (distinct from how a single agent calls a tool) are still actively being defined across the industry.

quiz.question: What is a key drawback of simply concatenating the full conversation history and passing it to every subsequent agent?
options: It always produces a parsing error
It burns context window and cost on irrelevant history and buries the specific information the next agent needs
It is technically impossible to implement
It has no drawbacks, it's the recommended approach

quiz.question: What is a 'structured handoff object' in multi-agent communication?
options: A raw, unformatted transcript of the whole conversation
A defined schema (like findings, open questions, confidence) that the next agent can reliably parse instead of raw text
A single shared database with no schema at all
A method that only works for two agents, never more

quiz.question: When is a shared memory or blackboard pattern most useful?
options: When only one agent will ever exist
When many agents need visibility into evolving shared state rather than a tightly controlled point-to-point handoff
When you want to minimize all communication between agents
Only for image-generation tasks

title: Task Decomposition and Delegation
content: A planner agent's job is to break a high-level goal into subtasks that specialist agents can execute, and getting the granularity right is one of the harder design decisions in a multi-agent system. This course covers the two failure directions: over-decomposition, where a task is split into so many tiny subtasks that the coordination overhead (deciding what to delegate next, passing state between steps, handling each handoff) costs more in latency and complexity than it saves, and under-decomposition, where a single agent is handed a task that's still too broad and heterogeneous, causing the same quality problems a single generalist agent has in the first place. You'll learn practical heuristics: decompose along genuinely different skill boundaries (research vs. writing vs. fact-checking) rather than arbitrary step counts, and delegate a subtask to a specialist agent only when that subtask needs meaningfully different instructions, tools, or context than the rest of the work -- if two 'subtasks' would use nearly identical prompts and tools, they probably belong to the same agent.

quiz.question: What is 'over-decomposition' in multi-agent task planning?
options: Splitting a task so finely that coordination overhead outweighs any benefit
Never splitting a task at all
Assigning every subtask to the same agent
A pattern that only applies to single-agent systems

quiz.question: What is a practical heuristic for deciding whether two subtasks should be handled by separate specialist agents?
options: Always split every task into exactly three subtasks
Split along genuinely different skill boundaries; if two subtasks would use nearly identical prompts and tools, keep them together
Split based on how many words the task description contains
Never split any task under any circumstances

quiz.question: What is the risk of under-decomposition?
options: Too much coordination overhead between agents
The same quality problems as a single overloaded generalist agent, since the subtask is still too broad
It always causes a system crash
It has no risks, more decomposition is always better

title: Handling Agent Failures and Runaway Loops
content: Multi-agent systems introduce a failure mode single-agent systems rarely see: runaway loops, where an agent (or a pair of agents handing off to each other) repeats the same unproductive action indefinitely -- calling the same tool with slightly varied arguments, or two agents endlessly 'discussing' without converging on an answer -- silently consuming tokens and money until something external stops it. This course covers the standard defenses: hard iteration limits (cap the number of steps or handoffs and force a fallback once reached), timeout and retry policies with backoff (distinguish a transient failure worth retrying from a persistent one that should stop the loop), circuit breakers (once a specific tool or agent has failed repeatedly, stop calling it and route around it instead of retrying blindly), and human-in-the-loop escalation (when automated recovery is exhausted, surface the state to a person rather than continuing to spend). You'll learn why monitoring token and cost consumption in real time, not just after the fact, matters specifically for multi-agent systems -- a runaway loop that would cost a few cents in a single-agent system can multiply across several looping agents into a very expensive bill before anyone notices.

quiz.question: Why are runaway loops a distinct concern in multi-agent systems compared to single-agent systems?
options: They can never happen in multi-agent systems
Two or more agents handing off to each other without converging can multiply cost and token usage much faster than a single agent looping alone
Multi-agent systems have no tools to call
Loops only affect latency, never cost

quiz.question: What does a circuit breaker do in this context?
options: It permanently shuts down the entire system after one failure
After a tool or agent fails repeatedly, it stops calling it and routes around it instead of blindly retrying
It increases the retry rate for failing components
It has nothing to do with failure handling

quiz.question: Why does real-time cost monitoring matter specifically for multi-agent systems?
options: Cost monitoring is irrelevant to multi-agent systems
A runaway loop across multiple agents can multiply into a large bill much faster than in a single-agent system, before anyone notices after the fact
Multi-agent systems never incur any cost
Monitoring only matters for single-agent deployments

title: Security Boundaries in Multi-Agent Systems
content: Every handoff between agents is a new opportunity for an attack to slip through, and this course covers why multi-agent systems need more deliberate security design than single-agent ones. Prompt injection risk compounds across handoffs: if agent A retrieves an untrusted document containing hidden instructions and passes its output to agent B without validation, agent B may execute those injected instructions believing they came from a trusted source, even if agent A's own prompt was well-defended. You'll learn the core mitigations: least-privilege permission scoping (give each agent access only to the specific tools and data it strictly needs for its role, so a compromised agent has limited blast radius), sandboxing tool execution (run risky actions like code execution or file access in an isolated environment with restricted permissions, not directly on production infrastructure), and validating outputs at each handoff boundary (treating another agent's output as untrusted input, the same way you'd treat user input, rather than assuming it's safe because it came from 'your own system'). The core mental shift this course builds: in a multi-agent system, trust doesn't automatically transfer across a handoff just because both sides are agents you built.

quiz.question: Why does prompt injection risk compound across agent handoffs?
options: It doesn't; injection risk is identical to single-agent systems
An agent can pass along injected instructions from an untrusted source, and a downstream agent may execute them believing they're trusted
Agents cannot pass any information to each other
Only the first agent in a chain can be compromised

quiz.question: What does 'least-privilege permission scoping' mean for multi-agent security?
options: Giving every agent full access to all tools and data for convenience
Giving each agent access only to the specific tools and data it strictly needs, limiting blast radius if compromised
Removing all permissions from every agent
A pattern that only applies to human users, not agents

quiz.question: Why should an agent's output be validated at a handoff boundary rather than trusted automatically?
options: Because outputs from your own agents are always safe by definition
Because another agent's output should be treated as untrusted input, just like user input, since trust doesn't automatically transfer across a handoff
Validation is unnecessary overhead with no security benefit
Only user input ever needs validation, never agent output

title: Multi-Agent Systems Certification Assessment
content: This capstone validates practical multi-agent systems judgment: choosing coordination patterns, decomposing tasks at the right granularity, defending against runaway loops, and securing handoffs between agents. Before attempting it you should be comfortable explaining when a task benefits from splitting across specialist agents versus when a single agent is sufficient, the tradeoffs between orchestrator and swarm coordination, and why trust does not automatically transfer across an agent handoff. The questions are scenario-driven: given a system where two agents are endlessly handing a task back and forth without converging, can you name the right defense? Given an agent that retrieves an untrusted document and passes its output downstream unchecked, can you identify the security gap? Passing signals you could design and debug a real multi-agent system, not just describe the concepts.

quiz.question: Two agents in a pipeline keep handing a task back and forth without ever converging on a final answer. What's the most direct fix?
options: Add more agents to the loop
Add a hard iteration limit with a fallback once it's reached
Increase each agent's context window
Nothing can be done about this

quiz.question: An agent retrieves an untrusted web document and passes its raw output to a second agent, which then executes a suggested action without checks. What is the security gap?
options: There is no gap; agent output is always safe
The second agent trusted unvalidated content from a handoff, allowing potential prompt injection to propagate
The gap is that too few agents were used
The gap is unrelated to security, only to cost

quiz.question: A task is genuinely complex with clearly distinct skill requirements (research, drafting, fact-checking). What does this suggest?
options: It should always be handled by a single generalist agent
It's a reasonable candidate for decomposition across specialist agents along those skill boundaries
It should never be automated at all
It requires a swarm pattern specifically, never an orchestrator

quiz.question: What is this capstone primarily assessing?
options: Memorization of agent framework names
Practical judgment about coordination, decomposition, failure handling, and security in multi-agent systems
Speed of writing prompts
Knowledge of an unrelated topic

title: Why Evaluating LLM Applications Is Different
content: Traditional software testing relies on deterministic assertions: given this input, the output must exactly equal that value. LLM applications break this model because the same prompt can produce different, and often equally valid, phrasings on different runs -- there frequently isn't one single 'correct' output to assert against. This course introduces the mental shift required: instead of binary pass/fail per test case, LLM evaluation typically works with rubrics (a set of criteria a good answer must satisfy, like 'cites the source document' or 'stays under 100 words'), reference-based scoring (comparing against one or more example-good answers using similarity rather than exact match), and aggregate pass rates across a test set rather than expecting 100% on every single case. You'll learn why this makes evaluation an ongoing statistical practice rather than a one-time gate: a prompt or model change might improve the pass rate from 82% to 88% overall while making a handful of previously-passing cases newly fail, and catching that kind of tradeoff requires running a consistent test set on every change, not just spot-checking a few examples by hand.

quiz.question: Why do exact-match assertions, common in traditional software testing, break down for LLM applications?
options: LLMs never produce text output
The same prompt can produce different, equally valid phrasings, so there often isn't one single correct output to match exactly
Exact-match assertions work perfectly fine for LLMs
LLM outputs are always identical across runs

quiz.question: What does it mean to think of LLM evaluation as an 'aggregate pass rate' rather than binary pass/fail?
options: Every single test case must pass or the system fails entirely
You track the percentage of a test set that meets rubric criteria, since perfect scores on every case aren't a realistic bar
Pass rates are irrelevant to LLM applications
This approach is only used for image models

quiz.question: Why might a prompt change that raises overall pass rate from 82% to 88% still be worth scrutinizing carefully?
options: A higher pass rate is always strictly better with no downside
It could newly break a handful of previously-passing cases even while improving the average, which only a consistent test set run on every change would catch
Pass rate changes are never meaningful
This scenario is impossible in practice

title: Building Golden Datasets and Test Sets
content: A golden dataset is a curated set of representative inputs paired with expert-verified expected outputs (or grading criteria), and it's the foundation every other evaluation technique builds on. This course covers what makes a golden dataset useful rather than superficial: it should include realistic examples pulled from actual usage (not just easy, hand-picked cases that make the system look good), deliberately include edge cases (ambiguous questions, missing information, unusual phrasing) that stress-test the system's failure modes, and include a handful of adversarial examples designed to probe specific known weaknesses (like a question designed to tempt the model into fabricating an answer when it should say 'I don't know'). You'll learn why a golden dataset needs versioning just like code: as your application changes -- new features, new document sources, new user populations -- the dataset that was representative six months ago may no longer reflect real usage, and evaluating against a stale dataset can give false confidence that a change is safe when it hasn't actually been tested against the traffic patterns that matter now.

quiz.question: Why is it a mistake to build a golden dataset only from easy, hand-picked examples?
options: Easy examples are cheaper to collect
It won't stress-test the system's real failure modes and can give false confidence
Golden datasets should never include real user data
This is actually the recommended practice

quiz.question: Why does a golden dataset need to be versioned and periodically refreshed?
options: Because datasets expire automatically after 30 days by convention
Because as an application's usage and data sources evolve, a stale dataset may no longer reflect real traffic, giving false confidence
Versioning has no real benefit for evaluation datasets
Golden datasets never need to change once created

quiz.question: What is the purpose of including adversarial examples in a golden dataset, such as a question designed to tempt fabrication?
options: To make the dataset artificially harder for no reason
To probe specific known weaknesses, like whether the model says 'I don't know' instead of fabricating an answer
Adversarial examples should never be included in evaluation
To test the speed of the retrieval system only

title: LLM-as-Judge: Scaling Evaluation Without Losing Trust
content: Human review of every model output doesn't scale, so many teams use a second LLM call to grade the first model's output against a rubric or reference answer -- a technique called LLM-as-judge. This course covers why it's useful (it can evaluate thousands of examples for a fraction of the cost and time of human review, and can be run automatically on every change) and its well-documented biases: position bias (in pairwise comparisons, the judge can favor whichever answer appears first or second, regardless of quality), verbosity bias (judges often rate longer answers as better even when they aren't more correct), and self-preference bias (a judge model can rate outputs from its own model family more favorably). You'll learn the standard mitigations: randomizing answer order in pairwise comparisons, explicitly instructing the judge to penalize unnecessary length, calibrating the judge periodically against a small human-labeled sample to check it still agrees with human judgment, and using a different model family as judge than the one being evaluated where self-preference bias is a concern.

quiz.question: What is 'position bias' in LLM-as-judge pairwise comparisons?
options: The judge always picks the technically correct answer
The judge can favor whichever answer appears first or second in the comparison, regardless of actual quality
Position bias only affects human graders, not LLM judges
It refers to the physical location of the server

quiz.question: Why should teams periodically calibrate an LLM judge against human-labeled samples?
options: Calibration is unnecessary once a judge prompt is written
To check the judge still agrees with human judgment and catch drift in its scoring over time
To make the judge run faster
To eliminate the need for a golden dataset entirely

quiz.question: Why might using a different model family as the judge help mitigate self-preference bias?
options: It has no effect on self-preference bias
A judge from the same family as the model being evaluated may systematically rate that model's own outputs more favorably
Different model families cannot be used as judges at all
Self-preference bias only occurs with human judges

title: Metrics Beyond Accuracy: Faithfulness, Cost, and Latency
content: Optimizing an LLM application for a single metric, like accuracy against a test set, can silently break something else that matters just as much to real users. This course covers the fuller set of dimensions worth tracking: faithfulness or groundedness (does the answer only make claims supported by available evidence, distinct from whether the answer happens to be correct by coincidence), helpfulness and relevance (does the response actually address what the user needed, separate from factual correctness), latency (how long a user waits, which shapes whether a product feels usable regardless of answer quality), cost per query (which determines whether a feature is economically viable at scale), and safety metrics like toxicity or policy-violation rate. You'll learn a concrete example of the tension: a prompt change that adds several reasoning steps might raise accuracy by 5 points on your test set while tripling latency and cost per query -- whether that's a good trade depends entirely on the product's context, and a team that only tracks accuracy will make that call blind to the other costs.

quiz.question: Why is 'faithfulness' a distinct metric from raw answer correctness?
options: They measure exactly the same thing
An answer can be coincidentally correct without being supported by the retrieved or available evidence
Faithfulness only applies to image outputs
Correctness is always a subset of faithfulness with no distinction

quiz.question: A prompt change raises accuracy by 5 points but triples latency and cost. Why is tracking only accuracy risky here?
options: Because accuracy is the only metric that ever matters
Because the team would make the tradeoff decision blind to costs that matter just as much to the product
Because latency and cost are unrelated to LLM applications
Tracking multiple metrics is never useful

quiz.question: Which of these is an example of a safety-related evaluation metric?
options: Number of tokens generated
Toxicity or policy-violation rate
Retrieval recall
Embedding dimensionality

title: Regression Testing for Prompts and Models
content: A small prompt tweak, a model version upgrade, or a change to a retrieval pipeline can silently regress behavior that used to work -- and without a systematic check, that regression often isn't caught until a user reports it. This course covers building CI-style evaluation suites: running your golden test set automatically on every prompt or model change, tracking metric deltas (not just an overall pass rate but per-category breakdowns, so a regression hidden inside a small subgroup of cases doesn't get averaged away), and gating deploys on a defined threshold (a prompt change that drops accuracy on a specific case category below an agreed bar blocks the release rather than shipping and hoping). You'll learn why model version upgrades deserve the same regression discipline as your own prompt changes -- a provider's 'improved' model update can change output formatting, verbosity, or reasoning style in ways that break a system tuned around the old model's quirks, even though the new model is better on the provider's own benchmarks.

quiz.question: Why is tracking only an overall pass rate insufficient for catching regressions?
options: Overall pass rate is always sufficient
A regression hidden in a small subgroup of cases can get averaged away and go unnoticed in the aggregate number
Pass rates cannot be tracked over time
Regressions never occur in LLM systems

quiz.question: Why should upgrading to a provider's newer model version go through the same regression testing as a prompt change?
options: Newer models are always strictly better with no risk
A model upgrade can change formatting, verbosity, or reasoning style in ways that break a system tuned around the old model's behavior
Model upgrades never affect application behavior
Regression testing only applies to prompt changes, never model changes

quiz.question: What does it mean to 'gate deploys on a defined threshold' in this context?
options: Deploying regardless of test results
Blocking a release if a change drops a metric below an agreed bar on the test set, rather than shipping and hoping
Only testing after the deploy has already happened
Removing the test suite before deploying

title: Adversarial and Red-Team Testing for LLM Applications
content: Standard evaluation checks whether a system does what it's supposed to do; red-teaming checks whether it can be made to do what it's not supposed to do. This course covers the main categories of adversarial testing for LLM applications: prompt injection attempts (inputs crafted to override the system's instructions, often hidden inside retrieved documents or user-supplied content), jailbreak attempts (multi-step conversational strategies designed to get a model to bypass its safety guidelines), and data exfiltration probes (testing whether a malicious input can trick an agent with tool access into leaking sensitive data through a tool call or an unexpected output channel). You'll learn why red-teaming needs to be a systematic, ongoing practice rather than a one-time pre-launch checkbox: new jailbreak and injection techniques are discovered continuously across the industry, a fix for one specific attack pattern rarely generalizes to variations of it, and any meaningful change to prompts, tools, or the underlying model can reopen previously-closed vulnerabilities, so the red-team test suite needs to run on a recurring basis just like your functional regression suite.

quiz.question: What is the core difference between standard evaluation and red-team testing?
options: They are the same thing under different names
Standard evaluation checks whether a system does what it should; red-teaming checks whether it can be made to do what it shouldn't
Red-teaming only applies to non-LLM software
Standard evaluation is more thorough than red-teaming in every case

quiz.question: Why is red-teaming best treated as an ongoing practice rather than a one-time pre-launch check?
options: Because new injection and jailbreak techniques are discovered continuously, and changes to prompts or models can reopen old vulnerabilities
