Because red-teaming becomes unnecessary once done a single time
Because attacks never evolve over time
Because red-teaming is only relevant during initial development

quiz.question: What is a 'data exfiltration probe' testing for in an agentic LLM application?
options: Whether the model can count tokens accurately
Whether a malicious input can trick an agent with tool access into leaking sensitive data through an unexpected channel
Whether the model's response time is acceptable
Whether the embedding model is properly indexed

title: What Are Agent Tools?
content: An agent tool is a function the model can choose to invoke -- like searching the web, querying a database, or sending an email -- described to the model with a name, a description of what it does, and a schema for its parameters, rather than something the model executes directly itself. This course covers the basic loop: the model reads the user's request plus the list of available tools and their descriptions, decides whether calling a tool would help, and if so outputs a structured request naming the tool and its arguments; your application code then actually executes that function (the model never runs code itself) and returns the result back to the model, which can use it to continue reasoning or produce a final answer. You'll learn why this is a fundamentally different capability than pure text generation: a model that can only generate text can describe what it would do, while a model with tool access can actually cause things to happen in the world -- look up a real-time price, modify a real record, send a real message -- which is exactly why tool access introduces new categories of risk that plain text generation doesn't have.

quiz.question: Who actually executes the function when a model 'calls a tool'?
options: The model executes the code directly itself
Your application code executes the function; the model only requests it be called with certain arguments
Neither; tool calls are purely symbolic and never run
The tool executes itself with no application code involved

quiz.question: What fundamentally distinguishes tool-using agents from models that only generate text?
options: Tool-using agents are always more accurate at pure text tasks
Tool-using agents can actually cause real-world effects (like modifying a record), not just describe what they would do
There is no meaningful difference
Tool use eliminates the need for any prompting

quiz.question: What information does a model need about a tool in order to decide whether and how to call it?
options: Only the tool's internal source code
The tool's name, a description of what it does, and a schema for its parameters
Nothing; models call tools randomly
The tool's execution time in milliseconds only

title: Function Calling Basics: Schemas, Parsing, and the Execution Loop
content: This course walks through the mechanics of function calling end to end: each tool is defined with a JSON schema describing its parameters (name, type, whether required, a description), the model outputs a structured call matching that schema when it decides to use the tool, your code parses and validates that structured output before executing anything, the function runs and produces a result, and that result is fed back into the model's context so it can continue the conversation or task with the new information. You'll learn how modern APIs handle multiple tool calls requested in a single turn (the model might request three lookups at once, which your code can potentially execute in parallel), and why validating the model's proposed arguments before execution matters -- a model can occasionally propose a malformed or nonsensical argument (a negative quantity, a nonexistent ID), and executing it directly without validation can cause real harm downstream, exactly the way you'd validate any external, untrusted input in traditional software.

quiz.question: What should happen to a model's proposed tool arguments before your code executes them?
options: They should be executed immediately with no checks
They should be parsed and validated, the same way you'd validate any untrusted external input
They should be ignored entirely
They should be re-sent to the model without ever executing

quiz.question: Why might a model request multiple tool calls in a single turn?
options: This is never possible with modern APIs
It may need several independent lookups at once, which can potentially be executed in parallel
Multiple tool calls always indicate a bug
Each turn is limited to exactly one tool call by definition

quiz.question: What defines a tool's expected parameters so the model can produce valid structured calls?
options: A JSON schema describing parameter names, types, and whether they're required
The tool's internal implementation code
A free-text paragraph with no formal structure
Nothing; the model guesses parameters freely

title: Designing Good Tool Schemas
content: A tool's schema is effectively a prompt the model reads before deciding whether and how to call it, and poorly designed schemas cause real failures: wrong tool selection, malformed arguments, or the model giving up on tool use entirely. This course covers the practical principles: give each tool a clear, specific name and description that distinguishes it from similar tools (two tools named 'search' and 'lookup' with vague, overlapping descriptions invite the model to guess wrong), use tight parameter typing rather than accepting loosely-typed free text wherever a constrained type (an enum, a number with bounds) is possible, since constraints reduce the space of invalid calls the model can produce, and write parameter descriptions that specify format and units explicitly (a 'date' parameter should say what format is expected, a 'price' parameter should say what currency). You'll learn a common anti-pattern: exposing many narrow, single-purpose tools that do almost the same thing (get_user_by_id, get_user_by_email, get_user_by_username) instead of consolidating into fewer, well-scoped tools with clear parameters (get_user with an identifier-type field) -- more tools means more opportunities for the model to pick the wrong one, especially as the tool list grows.

quiz.question: Why can having many narrow, overlapping tools (like get_user_by_id, get_user_by_email) hurt an agent's reliability?
options: It has no effect on reliability
More similar tools give the model more opportunities to pick the wrong one, especially as the tool list grows
Narrow tools are always faster to execute
Models can only ever see one tool at a time regardless of how many exist

quiz.question: Why prefer tight parameter typing (like an enum) over free text where possible?
options: Free text is always invalid JSON
Constrained types reduce the space of invalid or malformed calls the model can produce
Tight typing makes the tool run faster on the server
There's no benefit; typing is purely cosmetic

quiz.question: Why should a 'date' parameter's description explicitly state the expected format?
options: Format doesn't matter since all date formats are equivalent
Without an explicit format, the model may produce a date string that doesn't match what your code expects, causing parsing failures
Descriptions are ignored by the model entirely
Only numeric parameters need format specifications

title: Error Handling for Tool Calls
content: Tool calls fail in production for all the usual reasons software fails: network timeouts, invalid arguments, downstream services returning errors, rate limits. This course covers why returning a clear, structured error message back to the model -- rather than a raw stack trace, or worse, silently swallowing the failure and returning nothing -- lets the model adjust its next step intelligently: retry with corrected arguments, try an alternative tool, or tell the user it couldn't complete the request, instead of either crashing the whole interaction or confidently proceeding as if the tool had succeeded. You'll learn the difference between transient errors worth retrying automatically (a timeout, a rate limit with a retry-after header) and permanent errors that shouldn't be retried blindly (an invalid ID that will never become valid, a permissions error), and why unbounded automatic retries on a persistent failure is itself a runaway-loop risk -- you need a retry cap and a clear fallback path once it's exhausted, mirroring the same failure-handling discipline used in traditional distributed systems.

quiz.question: Why is returning a structured error message to the model better than silently swallowing a tool failure?
options: Silently swallowing failures is always the safer choice
A structured error lets the model adjust intelligently (retry, try an alternative, or inform the user) instead of proceeding as if it succeeded
Structured errors are only useful for human developers, never for models
There's no difference in outcome either way

quiz.question: What distinguishes a transient error from a permanent one in tool-call error handling?
options: There is no meaningful distinction
Transient errors (like timeouts) are worth retrying automatically; permanent errors (like an invalid ID) will never succeed on retry
Permanent errors should always be retried indefinitely
Transient errors should never be retried

quiz.question: Why does unbounded automatic retrying on a persistent tool failure pose a risk?
options: It has no risk since retries are always cheap
It can become a runaway-loop scenario, consuming tokens and time with no path to resolution unless capped with a fallback
Retrying is always instantaneous and free
This only applies to single-agent systems, not tool calls

title: Tool Selection at Scale: When You Have Dozens of Tools
content: An agent with five well-described tools rarely picks the wrong one; an agent with fifty tools frequently does, simply because the model has to hold every tool's name, description, and schema in context and reason about all of them at once for every single decision. This course covers strategies for scaling tool access without scaling confusion: tool retrieval, where you use a lightweight search step (often embedding-based, similar to RAG) to surface only the handful of tools likely relevant to the current request, rather than exposing the full catalog every turn; hierarchical tool routing, where a first, cheap classification step picks a broad category (e.g. 'billing', 'scheduling', 'search') and only then exposes the narrower set of tools within that category; and grouping related tools into coherent toolsets that get enabled or disabled together based on context, rather than managing relevance at the level of each individual tool. You'll learn the underlying principle connecting all three approaches: the model's tool-selection accuracy depends heavily on how much irrelevant option-space it has to filter through at decision time, so reducing the visible tool surface for any given request is often a bigger lever than improving any individual tool's description.

quiz.question: Why does an agent with fifty available tools tend to select the wrong one more often than an agent with five?
options: Larger tool counts always improve selection accuracy
The model has to reason about every tool's name, description, and schema at once, and more options increase the chance of picking wrong
Tool count has no effect on selection accuracy
This only happens with older, smaller models

quiz.question: What is 'tool retrieval' as a strategy for scaling tool access?
options: Exposing the entire tool catalog on every single turn
Using a lightweight search step to surface only the tools likely relevant to the current request
Removing tools permanently once the catalog grows too large
A method for compressing tool schemas into fewer bytes

quiz.question: What is the underlying principle connecting tool retrieval, hierarchical routing, and toolset grouping?
options: They all aim to increase the number of visible tools at once
Reducing the visible, irrelevant tool surface for a given request often improves selection accuracy more than refining any single tool's description
They are unrelated strategies with no shared principle
They all require fine-tuning a new model

title: Agent Skills and Composability
content: A 'skill' is a step up from a raw tool: a packaged bundle of instructions, examples, and often one or more underlying tools that together teach an agent how to competently perform a specific, reusable procedure -- like 'draft a customer refund email following our policy' or 'summarize a call transcript into structured notes' -- rather than exposing a single low-level function and hoping the model figures out the right sequence of calls and framing on its own every time. This course covers why skills matter as a design layer: they encode not just what a tool does but how and when to use it well, captured once by an expert and reused reliably across many invocations, instead of re-deriving that judgment from scratch in every prompt. You'll learn about composability -- skills that can invoke other skills, letting you build higher-level capabilities out of lower-level ones, similar to how software functions call other functions -- and the practical challenges this introduces at scale: skill discovery (how does an agent find the right skill among many available), versioning (what happens to agents relying on a skill when that skill's instructions change), and avoiding the same tool-selection confusion that plagues large flat tool lists, just one layer up.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a 'skill' from a raw, low-level tool?
options: A skill is simply a tool renamed for marketing purposes
A skill packages instructions, examples, and often tools together to teach an agent how to competently perform a reusable procedure, not just expose a single function
Skills cannot call any underlying tools
There is no meaningful distinction between the two

quiz.question: What does 'composability' mean in the context of agent skills?
options: Skills can invoke other skills, building higher-level capabilities out of lower-level ones
Skills must always be used in complete isolation from one another
Composability refers only to how skills are stored in a database
Skills cannot be combined under any circumstances

quiz.question: What challenge does skill versioning introduce at scale?
options: Versioning has no practical implications
Agents relying on a skill may behave differently or break when that skill's underlying instructions change
Versioning only matters for raw tools, never for skills
Skills never need to change once created

title: What Is Context Engineering?
content: Context engineering is the discipline of deciding exactly what information goes into a model's context window for a given call -- the system instructions, any retrieved documents, prior conversation history, tool definitions and their outputs, and the current user request -- and in what order and format, so the model has precisely what it needs and nothing that distracts from it. This course frames context engineering as broader than 'prompt engineering': prompt engineering typically focuses on how you word a single instruction, while context engineering is about architecting the whole assembly of information a model sees on every call, especially in systems with retrieval, tools, and multi-turn conversation where the context is dynamically built up rather than a single static prompt someone wrote once. You'll learn why this matters more as systems grow more complex: a simple single-turn Q&A prompt has little to architect, but an agent juggling retrieved documents, a long conversation history, several tool schemas, and evolving task state has a real design problem in deciding what's relevant enough to include, what to summarize, and what to drop, given a fixed and costly context budget.

quiz.question: How does context engineering differ from narrower 'prompt engineering'?
options: They are exactly the same practice
Context engineering is the broader discipline of architecting everything that goes into the context window, not just wording a single instruction
Prompt engineering only applies to image models
Context engineering only concerns system prompts, nothing else

quiz.question: Why does context engineering become a bigger design problem as systems grow more complex?
options: It doesn't; complexity has no bearing on context design
Systems with retrieval, tools, and long conversations must actively decide what's relevant, what to summarize, and what to drop within a fixed, costly context budget
More complex systems automatically have unlimited context windows
Context engineering only matters for the very first prompt in a conversation

quiz.question: What does context engineering include beyond just the system prompt?
options: Only the system prompt matters; everything else is irrelevant
Retrieved documents, conversation history, tool definitions and outputs, and the current request, in addition to system instructions
Only the user's most recent message
Nothing beyond the model's training data

title: System Prompts vs. User Prompts vs. Conversation History
content: Most chat-based LLM APIs distinguish between a system message (persistent instructions, persona, and constraints that should apply across the whole interaction), user messages (the specific request or question at a given turn), and, over a multi-turn conversation, an accumulating history of prior turns. This course covers how models tend to weight these differently -- system instructions are generally treated as higher-priority framing that should hold even as the conversation continues, while user messages carry the immediate task -- and the common mistake of cramming everything into the system prompt: a system prompt bloated with information that's really turn-specific (like details only relevant to the current question) becomes stale or irrelevant as the conversation moves on, while genuinely persistent rules get buried in a wall of situational detail. You'll learn the practical guideline: put durable behavior rules, persona, and constraints in the system prompt; put the actual task, question, and any turn-specific data in the user message; and let conversation history do the job of carrying forward what's actually been discussed, rather than re-stating it in the system prompt each time.

quiz.question: What is a common mistake when structuring system prompts?
options: Keeping them too short
Cramming turn-specific information into the system prompt, where it becomes stale and buries genuinely persistent rules
Never including any instructions at all
Only using system prompts for single-turn conversations

quiz.question: What content is best suited for the system prompt versus the user message?
options: Everything belongs in the system prompt regardless of type
Durable behavior rules, persona, and constraints belong in the system prompt; the actual task and turn-specific data belong in the user message
The user message should contain the persona and constraints
There's no meaningful distinction between the two message types

quiz.question: How do models generally treat system instructions relative to user messages over a conversation?
options: System instructions are ignored after the first turn
System instructions are generally treated as higher-priority framing that should hold throughout the conversation
User messages always override system instructions completely
There's no difference in how either is weighted

title: Context Window Budgeting
content: Every token in a model's context window costs money and competes for the model's limited attention, so treating the context window as a scarce, deliberately allocated budget -- rather than an unlimited scratchpad -- is a core context engineering skill. This course covers how to think about allocating that budget across competing needs: system instructions and tool schemas (often fixed, paid on every call), retrieved knowledge (variable, should scale with how much evidence the query genuinely needs, not a fixed chunk count regardless of question complexity), conversation history (grows unboundedly over a long session unless actively managed), and headroom for the model's own output. You'll learn practical budgeting techniques: setting explicit token caps per section, truncating or summarizing the oldest conversation turns once a threshold is hit rather than letting history grow unchecked, and dynamically adjusting how many retrieved chunks to include based on a relevance-score cutoff rather than always including a fixed top-k regardless of how relevant they actually are. The core skill this course builds: recognizing when a system's cost or quality problems trace back to poor context budgeting -- too much irrelevant history, too many low-relevance retrieved chunks -- rather than the underlying model being inadequate.

quiz.question: Why should context window allocation be treated as a deliberate budget rather than an unlimited scratchpad?
options: Context windows are free and unlimited in practice
Every token costs money and competes for the model's limited attention, so allocation choices directly affect cost and quality
Budgeting only matters for image-based models
There is no cost associated with context length

quiz.question: Why is always including a fixed top-k number of retrieved chunks, regardless of relevance, a weaker approach than a relevance-score cutoff?
options: Fixed top-k is always the better approach
It can include low-relevance chunks that waste budget on queries needing little evidence, or omit needed evidence on queries needing more
Relevance scores are never available in retrieval systems
Chunk count has no effect on context budget

quiz.question: A system's answers are getting worse and slower as conversations get longer. What is a likely context-budgeting culprit?
options: The model has stopped working entirely
Unbounded conversation history is accumulating and crowding out budget for more relevant content
This can only be caused by a change in the underlying model
Longer conversations always improve answer quality with no downside

title: Memory and State Management for Conversational Agents
content: Conversational agents need to track two different kinds of memory: short-term memory, the state relevant to the current session (what's been discussed in this conversation so far), and long-term memory, information that should persist and be recalled across separate sessions (a user's stated preferences, past decisions, ongoing project context). This course covers common techniques for each: a sliding window that keeps only the most recent N turns in context, summarization buffers that periodically condense older turns into a compact summary rather than dropping them entirely, and external memory stores (often a simple database or a vector store) that hold long-term facts the agent can retrieve when relevant, rather than trying to keep everything in the live context window indefinitely. You'll learn a real risk with long-term memory that's easy to overlook: stale or incorrect information persisting across sessions can actively mislead an agent later -- if a user's preference or a fact changes and the memory store isn't updated or invalidated, the agent may confidently apply outdated information in a later session, which can be harder to detect and debug than a single-session context problem because the wrong information didn't even originate in the current conversation.

quiz.question: What is the difference between short-term and long-term memory for a conversational agent?
options: There is no meaningful difference
Short-term memory covers the current session's state; long-term memory persists and is recalled across separate sessions
Long-term memory only applies to a single conversation turn
Short-term memory is always stored in a vector database

quiz.question: What is a real risk of long-term memory stores that's easy to overlook?
options: Long-term memory has no risks at all
Stale or incorrect information can persist across sessions and mislead the agent later, in a way that's hard to trace back to its origin
Long-term memory always self-corrects automatically
Long-term memory can only ever improve agent performance

quiz.question: What does a summarization buffer do that a plain sliding window doesn't?
options: It discards all older turns with no trace
It condenses older turns into a compact summary rather than dropping them entirely, preserving some information as context grows
It has an identical effect to a sliding window
It only applies to system prompts

title: Context Compression Techniques
content: As conversations, retrieved evidence, and tool outputs accumulate, keeping every raw token in context becomes expensive and eventually infeasible, so this course covers techniques for compressing context while preserving what actually matters. Summarizing older turns condenses a long transcript into a shorter representation of what was discussed, trading some nuance and exact wording for a large reduction in token count. Extracting structured facts goes further, pulling out just the specific data points a later step will need (like a set of key-value facts established earlier in the conversation) rather than keeping a prose summary at all, which is often more reliable for information a downstream step needs to use precisely. Prompt caching, offered by several providers, lets you avoid recomputing and re-paying for a stable prefix (like a long system prompt or a set of few-shot examples) across repeated calls, which isn't compression in the traditional sense but achieves a similar practical goal of not re-processing the same context repeatedly. You'll learn the central tradeoff underlying all compression: the more aggressively you compress, the more you risk losing a specific detail that turns out to matter later, so compression decisions should be informed by what a task is likely to need, not applied uniformly regardless of context.

quiz.question: What is the central tradeoff involved in context compression?
options: Compression has no tradeoffs; more compression is always better
More aggressive compression risks losing specific details that may matter later, so it should be informed by what a task actually needs
Compression always improves accuracy with no cost
Compression only affects latency, never accuracy

quiz.question: Why might extracting structured facts be more reliable than a prose summary for information a downstream step needs precisely?
options: Prose summaries always retain more precision
Structured extraction pulls out specific data points cleanly rather than relying on a summary that may paraphrase or drop exact values
Structured facts cannot be stored or retrieved later
There's no difference between the two approaches

quiz.question: How does prompt caching relate to context compression, even though it isn't compression in the traditional sense?
options: It has no relationship to context management at all
It avoids recomputing and re-paying for a stable prefix across repeated calls, achieving a similar practical goal of not reprocessing the same context
It permanently deletes old context from the model
It only works for retrieved documents, never system prompts

title: Multi-Turn Context Drift and the 'Lost in the Middle' Effect
content: Long conversations and long contexts don't just cost more -- they can measurably degrade an agent's behavior, a phenomenon this course covers under two related ideas. Context drift describes how, over many turns, a conversation can accumulate noise, tangents, and even outright contradictions (a user changes their mind, or an earlier assumption turns out to be wrong), and if the agent keeps weighing everything in the accumulated history equally, its behavior can drift away from the current, correct state of the task. The 'lost in the middle' effect describes a documented tendency for models to attend more reliably to information near the beginning and end of a long context than to content buried in the middle, meaning a critical instruction or fact placed in the middle of a very long prompt can be effectively under-weighted even though it's technically present. You'll learn practical mitigations for both: periodically re-injecting key instructions or the current, corrected state near the end of the context (closer to where the model is about to generate) rather than relying on something stated many turns ago, and actively pruning or correcting outdated information from history instead of letting contradictions accumulate silently.

quiz.question: What is the 'lost in the middle' effect?
options: Models perform equally well regardless of where information sits in a long context
A documented tendency for models to attend less reliably to information placed in the middle of a long context compared to the beginning or end
A bug that only affects very short prompts
An effect that only applies to system prompts, never user content

quiz.question: Why can 'context drift' cause an agent to behave incorrectly even though the correct information was stated earlier in the conversation?
options: The correct information is always weighted most heavily automatically
If contradictions or outdated assumptions accumulate and are weighed equally with corrected information, the agent's behavior can drift away from the current correct state
Context drift is not a real phenomenon
Longer conversations always improve accuracy over time

quiz.question: What is a practical mitigation for the 'lost in the middle' effect on a critical instruction?
options: Removing the instruction from the prompt entirely
Re-injecting the key instruction closer to the end of the context, nearer to where the model is about to generate
Always placing critical instructions in the exact middle of the prompt
Increasing temperature to compensate

title: Context Engineering Certification Assessment
content: This capstone validates practical context engineering judgment: architecting what goes into a model's context, budgeting a limited context window across competing needs, managing memory across sessions, and recognizing degradation from context drift or the 'lost in the middle' effect. Before attempting it you should be comfortable explaining the difference between prompt engineering and context engineering, how to allocate context budget across system instructions, retrieved knowledge, and history, and why compression and memory management both carry a real risk of losing or misapplying information. The questions are scenario-driven: given a long-running agent whose behavior degrades over a lengthy conversation, can you diagnose whether the cause is context drift, budget exhaustion, or a 'lost in the middle' placement issue, and propose the right fix? Passing signals you could debug a real context-management problem in production, not just define the terms.

quiz.question: An agent's answers become inconsistent and occasionally contradict earlier correct statements as a conversation grows very long. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model has run out of storage space
Context drift, where accumulated noise and contradictions in history are being weighed alongside corrected information
This is always caused by a hardware failure
Long conversations never affect agent behavior

quiz.question: A critical instruction placed in the middle of a very long system prompt is being followed inconsistently. What is a likely explanation and fix?
options: The instruction should be removed since it's clearly wrong
The 'lost in the middle' effect; moving or re-injecting the instruction closer to the end of the context can help
This is unrelated to context placement and can't be fixed
Adding more unrelated content will resolve it

quiz.question: A system's cost and latency are climbing over a long session while quality also degrades. Where should you look first?
options: The underlying model must be replaced immediately
Context budgeting: unbounded history or excessive retrieved content may be crowding out relevant, current information
This can only be a network issue
Nothing can be done once a session grows long

quiz.question: What is this capstone primarily assessing?
options: Memorization of context engineering terminology
Practical judgment in diagnosing and fixing real context-management problems in a running system
Speed of prompt writing
Knowledge of an unrelated domain

title: How Token Pricing Works
content: Most LLM providers price API usage per token, typically quoted as a rate per one million tokens, and understanding this billing unit is the foundation for every cost decision that follows. This course covers the basic calculation: total cost for a request equals input tokens processed times the input rate, plus output tokens generated times the output rate, and these two rates are usually different from each other. You'll walk through a concrete example: if a provider charges $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, a request with a 2,000-token prompt and a 500-token response costs roughly (2,000 / 1,000,000 x $3) + (500 / 1,000,000 x $15) -- about $0.006 for input plus $0.0075 for output, around $0.0135 total, which sounds trivial per call but adds up quickly at scale: a feature serving 100,000 requests a day at that rate is already over $1,300 a day. You'll learn why teams need to estimate token counts before shipping a feature, not just track spend after the fact, since a seemingly small per-request cost can become a large recurring expense once multiplied by real usage volume.

quiz.question: What are the two main components of the cost formula for a single LLM API request?
options: Only the number of input tokens matters
Input tokens times the input rate, plus output tokens times the output rate
A flat fee regardless of token count
Cost is based solely on latency, not tokens

quiz.question: Why do input and output tokens typically have different prices?
options: They are always priced identically
Providers set separate rates, and output tokens are usually priced higher reflecting the cost of generation
Input tokens are never billed at all
Pricing is randomly assigned per request

quiz.question: Why is it important to estimate token costs before shipping a feature, not just track spend afterward?
options: Pre-launch estimation is unnecessary since costs are always negligible
A small per-request cost can become a large recurring expense once multiplied by real usage volume, and estimating ahead avoids surprises
Token costs cannot be estimated in advance under any circumstances
Only output tokens ever need to be considered

title: Input vs. Output Token Costs: Why They Differ
content: Across most providers, output tokens cost noticeably more per token than input tokens, often several times as much, and this course explains why that asymmetry exists and what it implies for how you design a system. Processing input tokens (the 'prefill' stage) can largely happen in parallel -- the model can process the entire prompt's tokens together in one pass. Generating output tokens happens autoregressively, one token at a time, where each new token depends on all the previous ones, making generation inherently more sequential and computationally expensive per token. You'll learn the practical design implication: a verbose system that generates long explanations, extensive reasoning traces, or repeats large amounts of input back in its output pays a disproportionate cost penalty compared to a system that's equally accurate but concise, and instructing a model to be appropriately brief (or asking for a structured, compact output format like a short JSON object instead of a long prose explanation) can meaningfully reduce cost without meaningfully reducing quality, in tasks where verbosity wasn't actually adding value.

quiz.question: Why is generating output tokens generally more expensive per token than processing input tokens?
options: Output tokens are billed the same as input tokens everywhere
Output generation happens sequentially, one token depending on the previous ones, making it inherently more computationally expensive per token than parallel input processing
Input tokens require more memory than output tokens
There is no cost difference between input and output tokens

quiz.question: What is a practical cost-saving implication of the input/output pricing asymmetry?
options: Always maximize output length regardless of task
Instructing a model to be appropriately concise or using a compact output format can meaningfully reduce cost without reducing quality where verbosity wasn't adding value
Input length has no bearing on cost at all
Output pricing asymmetry is irrelevant to system design

quiz.question: Why can processing input tokens happen largely in parallel while output token generation cannot?
options: Input and output are processed identically
The model can process an entire prompt's tokens together in one pass, while each generated output token depends on all previous ones
Parallel processing is only possible for output tokens
This distinction doesn't actually exist

title: Prompt Caching and Cost Savings
content: Many API calls share a large, stable prefix -- a long system prompt, a set of few-shot examples, a big block of reference material -- that's identical across many separate requests, and prompt caching lets a provider avoid reprocessing that shared prefix every single time, passing much of the savings on to you at a substantially reduced rate for the cached portion. This course covers how caching typically works in practice: the provider recognizes when a new request's beginning matches a previously-processed prompt exactly, reuses the already-computed internal representation for that matching prefix, and only pays full processing cost for the new, variable content appended after it. You'll learn the practical implication for how you structure prompts: to benefit from caching, put the stable, unchanging content first (system instructions, few-shot examples, static reference documents) and put the variable, request-specific content last (the current user question, request-specific data) -- reordering a prompt so the variable part comes first, even if the content is otherwise identical, can break the cache match and eliminate the savings entirely.

quiz.question: What does prompt caching typically require in order to produce cost savings?
options: Every request must be completely identical, including the variable parts
A stable, unchanging prefix shared across requests that the provider can recognize and reuse without reprocessing
Caching works regardless of prompt structure
Caching only applies to output tokens, never input

quiz.question: Why should stable content (like system instructions) be placed before variable content (like the user's specific question) in a prompt to benefit from caching?
options: Order has no effect on caching behavior
Caching relies on matching a prefix exactly; putting variable content first would break the prefix match and eliminate savings
Variable content should always come first for caching to work
Caching only works if there is no variable content at all

quiz.question: What is the main cost benefit of prompt caching?
options: It eliminates all API costs entirely
It substantially reduces the cost of reprocessing a shared, stable prefix across multiple requests
It only reduces latency, never cost
It doubles the cost of every request as a tradeoff for speed

title: Choosing Models for Cost Efficiency: Routing and Cascading
content: Not every request in a real application needs the most capable, most expensive model available, and this course covers model routing (also called cascading): using a cheap, fast model to handle the easy majority of requests, and escalating only the genuinely hard cases to a more expensive, more capable model. A common pattern is a lightweight classifier or the cheap model itself attempting the task first with a confidence signal -- if confidence is high, return that answer; if confidence is low or the task is flagged as complex, re-route the request to a stronger model. You'll learn how to think about the cost-quality tradeoff curve this creates: routing well can capture most of the cost savings of always using the cheap model while capturing most of the quality of always using the expensive model, but routing poorly (a bad confidence signal, or a classifier that itself costs meaningfully more than the savings it's supposed to protect) can end up costing more than just picking one model consistently. The judgment call this course builds: recognizing when the added complexity and failure modes of a routing system are worth it for the cost savings at your actual traffic volume and difficulty distribution, versus when it's premature optimization for a system that doesn't have enough scale or difficulty variance to benefit.

quiz.question: What is the core idea behind model routing or cascading for cost efficiency?
options: Always using the most expensive model for every request
Using a cheap model for easy requests and escalating only genuinely hard cases to a more expensive model
Randomly assigning models to requests with no logic
Using the cheapest model for every request regardless of difficulty

quiz.question: What can make a routing system end up costing more than just using one model consistently?
options: Routing systems always save money with no downside
A poor confidence signal or an expensive classification step can itself cost more than the savings it's meant to protect
Routing is always free to implement
This scenario is impossible in practice

quiz.question: When might model routing be premature optimization rather than a worthwhile investment?
options: When traffic volume and task difficulty variance are too low to generate meaningful savings relative to the added complexity
Routing is always worthwhile regardless of scale
Only when using open-weight models
Routing should always be implemented from day one

title: Batch Processing for Cost Reduction
content: Several major providers offer a batch or asynchronous API mode that processes requests within a longer completion window (often within 24 hours) in exchange for a substantially discounted rate, commonly around half the price of real-time synchronous calls. This course covers when this tradeoff makes sense: workloads that are not latency-sensitive, like nightly re-scoring of a large document set, bulk classification of historical records, or generating a large batch of evaluation results, are ideal candidates, since the delay costs nothing in user experience but the discount meaningfully reduces spend at scale. You'll learn the corresponding limitations: batch mode typically doesn't support streaming responses back token-by-token, isn't suitable for anything with a real-time user waiting on the other end, and often has its own submission and result-retrieval mechanics distinct from the standard real-time API, requiring separate application logic to handle. You'll leave able to correctly classify a given workload as batch-appropriate or not, based on whether a delayed result is actually acceptable for that use case, not just based on the cost savings alone.

quiz.question: What is the main tradeoff of using a batch or asynchronous API mode?
options: Higher cost in exchange for faster results
A substantially discounted rate in exchange for accepting a longer completion window and no real-time streaming
No tradeoff; batch mode is strictly better in every way
Batch mode only works with open-weight models

quiz.question: Which workload is a good candidate for batch processing?
options: A real-time customer-facing chat interface
Nightly re-scoring of a large historical document set with no user waiting on the result
A live voice assistant
Any workload requiring immediate streamed responses

quiz.question: Why is batch mode unsuitable for a real-time user-facing chat feature?
options: Batch mode is actually faster than real-time APIs
Batch mode doesn't support streaming and can take up to a completion window (often 24 hours), incompatible with a user waiting live
Real-time features cannot use LLMs at all
There is no difference between batch and real-time modes

title: Monitoring and Budgeting for LLM Spend
content: As LLM features move from prototype to production, spend can grow unpredictably and silently unless it's actively monitored, and this course covers the practices that keep it under control. Per-request cost tracking (logging token counts and computed cost alongside every call, tagged with the feature, user, or team responsible) is the foundation, since without attribution you can see total spend rising but not know which feature or which change caused it. Alerting on spend anomalies (a sudden spike well above the historical baseline, which often signals a runaway agent loop, a bug causing retries, or an unexpected traffic surge) lets you catch cost problems within hours instead of discovering them at the end of a billing cycle. You'll learn why forecasting future spend as usage scales matters for planning, not just reacting: a feature that costs $50 a day at your current 1,000 daily users may cost $5,000 a day at 100,000 users, and understanding that scaling relationship before you hit it lets you make deliberate cost-efficiency investments (caching, routing, smaller models for simple cases) ahead of time rather than in a reactive scramble once a bill arrives that's ten times larger than expected.

quiz.question: Why does per-request cost tracking need to be tagged with a feature, user, or team, rather than just tracking total spend?
options: Tagging has no practical benefit over a single total number
Without attribution, you can see total spend rising but not identify which feature or change is responsible
Total spend tracking is always sufficient on its own
Tagging is only useful for billing disputes with the provider

quiz.question: What does an unexpected spike in LLM spend, well above the historical baseline, often signal?
options: Spend spikes are always random and meaningless
A runaway agent loop, a retry bug, or an unexpected traffic surge worth investigating
Spend spikes only ever indicate normal, expected growth
This can only be caused by a pricing change from the provider

quiz.question: Why is forecasting future spend as usage scales valuable, beyond just monitoring current spend?
options: Forecasting has no practical value since costs are always linear and predictable
It reveals scaling relationships (like cost per user growing with volume) early enough to invest deliberately in cost-efficiency measures before a large unexpected bill arrives
Forecasting is only relevant to providers, not application teams
Current spend monitoring alone is always sufficient for planning

title: Agentic Systems Bootcamp: Coordinating Multiple Agents
content: A bundled sequence introducing multi-agent systems from first principles: what a multi-agent system is and when splitting work across specialist agents beats a single generalist agent, the tradeoffs between centralized orchestration and decentralized swarm coordination, and how agents actually pass state and results to one another without drowning each other in irrelevant context. Complete the linked courses in order to build a foundation before tackling failure handling and security in the advanced Multi-Agent Systems courses.

title: Context and Cost Fundamentals: Making Every Token Count
content: A bundled sequence connecting two disciplines that are really two sides of the same coin: what actually goes into a model's context window, and what that context costs you in tokens and dollars. Covers the fundamentals of context engineering, how to budget a limited context window deliberately, and how token-based pricing actually works, so you can reason about both quality and cost tradeoffs together rather than treating them as separate concerns. Complete the linked courses in order.
